baseProblem.statement: You're climbing a staircase with n steps. You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways can you reach the top?

rounds.question: Why does ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2)?
options: Because the staircase has exactly two sides
Because the last step taken was either a 1-step (from n−1) or a 2-step (from n−2), and those are disjoint paths
Because you alternate 1-steps and 2-steps
Because n is always even or odd
rounds.explanation: Every path to n ends with either a 1-step or a 2-step. Counting separately and summing covers all paths without double-counting.

rounds.question: What's the most space-efficient way to compute ways(n) iteratively?
options: Build a full array of size n+1 and read array[n] at the end
Recurse with memoization in a hash map
Track only the previous two values and roll forward
Compute using the closed-form Fibonacci formula
rounds.explanation: You only ever need the last two values to compute the next. O(1) space, no array needed.

rounds.question: What's the time complexity of the iterative O(1)-space approach?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(2ⁿ)
rounds.explanation: One pass from 2 to n, constant work per step. Total: O(n).

rounds.question: A teammate says: 'Just use recursion — ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2).' What's the problem with that as written?
options: Recursion is forbidden in production code
Without memoization it recomputes the same subproblems exponentially many times — O(2ⁿ)
Recursion can't compute Fibonacci-like sequences correctly
The base case is ambiguous
rounds.explanation: Pure recursion here is the canonical example of overlapping subproblems. Memoization or iteration fixes it; the recursive structure itself is fine.

rounds.question: Which input is most likely to expose a base case bug?
options: n = 0 (zero steps)
n = 1 (one step)
n = 45 (large enough to overflow naive recursion's stack)
n = 10 (typical case)
rounds.explanation: n = 0 is the underspecified case — is there 1 way (do nothing) or 0 ways (no staircase)? Naive implementations crash or return wrong values depending on how they're seeded.
